extracted.intended_audience: media and communication scholars, graduate students and researchers studying agenda‑setting and media effects
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological standards for conducting and evaluating empirical agenda‑setting research (how media coverage relates to public problem perception, including first/second/third‑level effects, intermedia influence, and appropriate analytic methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda‑Setting hypothesis (focus on cognitive effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: „Ihre ‚Agenda‑Setting‘‑Hypothese, damals bemerkenswert wegen ihrer Abkehr von der klassischen Persuasionsannahme und der Betonung kognitiver Effekte...“
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether research treats media influence as changing issue salience (cognitive accessibility) rather than direct persuasion of attitudes/choices. Studies should articulate whether they test salience effects and justify theoretical distinction from persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairing content analysis with audience surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: „Die Gegenüberstellung von Inhaltsanalyse und Publikumsbefragung ist, ... bis heute das Vorbild für die meisten empirischen Agenda‑Setting‑Studien."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological standard: empirical agenda‑setting studies should compare media content measures (e.g., frequency/front‑page prominence) with measures of public issue salience from surveys. Guidance: ensure content and survey measures are comparable in issue definitions and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalization of the criterion variable (public agenda)
rubrics_metrics.description: Referencing literature such as Edelstein (1993) and Jennings & Wlezien (2011) on thinking/distinguishing the criterion variable and between 'most important problems' and 'issues'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully define and justify the dependent variable (e.g., 'most important problem' vs. issue salience). Distinguish constructs and measurement instruments; report validity and sensitivity of measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: First‑level (issue salience) versus second‑level (attribute/image) effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Mentions of 'Second‑Level Agenda‑Setting' and works on candidate images and attributes (McCombs et al. 2000; Llamas et al.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify whether the study examines issue salience (what to think about) or attribute salience/framing (how to think about it). Use appropriate measures for attributes/images when testing second‑level effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of a 'third level' or expanded perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to 'An expanded perspective on Agenda‑Setting effects. Exploring the third level of Agenda Setting' (Guo, Vu & McCombs 2012).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to multi‑level conceptualizations beyond issue and attribute salience (e.g., network/relational effects). Describe what the 'third level' entails and operationalize accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermedia agenda‑setting and cross‑platform influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples such as 'Intermedia Agenda Setting between the New York Times and Twitter' and studies of intermedia influence using time series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying agenda flows, include multiple media sources (traditional and social). Use designs that can identify directional influence between outlets/platforms (e.g., lagged analyses, cross‑correlations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of time series and longitudinal methods to identify influence
rubrics_metrics.description: References to Meraz (2011), Kushin (2010) and other work using time series analysis to measure intermedia influence and dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For temporal/influence claims, use appropriate time series or panel methods with sufficient temporal resolution and tests for Granger causality or equivalent. Report stationarity checks, lags, and robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of advanced multivariate models (e.g., structural equation modeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mention of 'Structural equation models for the analysis of the Agenda‑Setting process' (Hügel, Degenhardt & Weiss 1989).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider SEM or comparable path models to model complex relationships (media agenda → public agenda → mediators) and to test indirect effects; report model fit and identification details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for real‑world cues and confounders
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations such as Erbring, Goldenberg & Miller (1980) on 'Front‑page news and real‑world cues' and other studies highlighting external influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control for real‑world events, elite cues, or other non‑media drivers of public salience. Design studies to separate media effects from coincident external events (e.g., by using content controls, instrumental variables, or natural experiments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling functional form: linear vs nonlinear relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to 'Linear and nonlinear models of Agenda‑Setting in television' (Brosius & Kepplinger 1992).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether media‑public relationships are linear or nonlinear (thresholds, diminishing returns). Explore model specifications and report comparative fits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue competition and zero‑sum attention (attention dynamics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to 'Issue competition and attention distraction: A zero‑sum theory of Agenda‑Setting' (Zhu 1992) and related literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider that public attention may be a limited resource; model competition between issues (zero‑sum effects) and test for displacement/attention tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal dynamics and decay of effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Works such as Watt, Mazza & Snyder (1993) on 'effects decay curve' are cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate how long agenda‑setting effects persist; include lag structures and decay functions, and report temporal robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptual and individual agenda‑designing processes
rubrics_metrics.description: References to perceptual phenomena and individual agenda‑designing (Rössler 1999; Huck, Quiring & Brosius 2009).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for individual‑level processes (interpersonal communication, egocentric networks, perception biases) that mediate or moderate media effects; include multi‑level or survey measures where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media convergence and multimedia contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Mention of 'Agenda‑Setting in der multimedialen Medienwelt' and works on media complementarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In contemporary studies, include multiple media modalities and consider complementarity/interaction effects across platforms rather than treating media as a single homogeneous source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content/argumentation structure analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to analyses of 'massenmediale Argumentationsstrukturen' and content dimensions (Weiss 1989).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond frequency counts, analyze qualitative content features (frames, arguments, tone) that shape salience and attribute salience; report coding schemes, reliability, and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical situating and cumulative research stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations to Neuman & Guggenheim (2011) on the evolution of media effects theory and to works that map the anatomy of agenda‑setting research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place empirical work within the cumulative trajectory of agenda‑setting theory; explicitly state which stage/variant of theory the study tests and how it contributes to theory development.
